opus-5.5.text:
I think we're at an interesting turning point. AI can already handle a lot of the "execution" side of research: writing code, running experiments, sweeping hyperparameters, summarizing papers, even drafting parts of a manuscript. A lot of a junior researcher's daily work, the engineering and the trial-and-error loops, is becoming automatable. That's a real productivity gain, because you can test many more ideas in the same amount of time.

The harder question is whether AI can do the part that really matters: deciding *what* to work on, and noticing when something surprising is actually important. Research isn't just optimization toward a known goal. Often the breakthrough comes from someone looking at a weird result everyone else ignored and asking, "Why does this happen?" Current models are very good at interpolating within the distribution of what humans have already written. They're less good at forming a new abstraction that wasn't in the training data, or at holding a long chain of reasoning that stays consistent over weeks of exploration.

So my view is that in the near term, the human role shifts upward. Researchers become more like directors or "taste-makers." You set the questions, judge which results are meaningful, and let AI agents do the heavy lifting underneath. That also means the bar for a good researcher changes. Raw implementation skill matters less, and insight, judgment, and the ability to ask good questions matter more.

Longer term, I'm actually quite interested in whether we can understand *how* models learn representations, which is part of why I work on theory. If we understand the mechanism by which neural networks discover structure, we might design systems that discover genuinely new concepts rather than just recombining old ones. That would be when AI truly starts automating discovery, not just research labor. We're not there yet, but I don't think it's as far away as many people assume.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify humans’ biological needs as limiting the time they can devote to research.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes automating research execution and routine labor from independently choosing important questions and discovering genuinely new concepts.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that research automation is happening in layers, and the layers are being automated at very different speeds.

The outermost layer is the mechanical stuff: writing code, running experiments, sweeping hyperparameters, reading and summarizing papers. That part is already largely automated, or at least it's becoming cheap enough that it doesn't bottleneck anyone anymore. A good agent today can take a rough idea, implement a baseline, and give you results overnight. That alone changes the economics of research, because the cost of trying something is dropping toward zero.

The middle layer is what I'd call hypothesis generation and verification. Can the system look at a set of experimental results, notice something anomalous, and propose a reason? This is where things get more interesting, and it's where I spend a lot of my own time. Models are actually decent at it in narrow settings. If you give them a well-defined search space, like finding a better optimizer or a better architecture variant, they can run a genuine loop of propose, test, revise. The problem is that the search space is usually defined by a human, and defining it correctly is most of the intellectual work.

That brings me to the innermost layer, which is knowing which question is worth asking. That's taste. It's a kind of compressed experience about what will matter in two years versus what's just locally interesting. I don't think current systems have that yet, and I'm not sure it emerges simply from scaling. It might require models that have a lot of interaction with the world, that have been wrong many times and learned from it, the way a graduate student becomes a researcher.

So my view is that the near-term picture is something like a lab with one or two people who have good taste, and a very large number of AI agents doing everything downstream of that. Research throughput goes up enormously, but the scarce resource shifts from execution to judgment. Longer term, whether the judgment layer gets automated too is the real open question, and I'd rather not pretend I know the answer.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify humans’ biological needs as limiting the time they can devote to research.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes automating mechanical research tasks from automating judgment about which questions are worth asking, which it says current systems lack.

astra-6.text:
I think AI will automate more and more parts of research, but the interesting question is whether it can close the entire loop. Research is not just answering a question. You have to decide which question matters, formulate a hypothesis, design an experiment, interpret the result, and then decide what to try next.

AI can help a lot when there is a clear way to evaluate progress. If you can run a program or test a prediction in a simulator, the system can propose ideas, get feedback, and improve. But in scientific discovery, feedback can be expensive or ambiguous. An experiment might take weeks, and a failed experiment doesn’t necessarily tell you whether the hypothesis was wrong or the experiment was poorly designed.

So I see human–AI collaboration as a very important stage. AI can expand the space of possibilities we explore and handle much of the implementation work. Humans can help choose meaningful problems and scrutinize the evidence. Over time, the system may take on more of that judgment too, but generating a plausible idea and establishing a reliable discovery are still different things.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human roles in choosing problems and scrutinizing evidence, but does not identify humans’ biological needs or limits on time devoted to research.

r002.rationale: The response says AI can handle implementation work and distinguishes plausible ideas from reliable discoveries, but it does not clearly contrast automating tedious research labor with independently discovering new insights.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI can automate more and more of the research process, but there’s a difference between solving a well-defined problem and figuring out what problem is worth solving. If you already have a clear objective and a way to evaluate the result, AI can help generate hypotheses, write code, run experiments, and analyze what happened. You can imagine that becoming a loop, where the system uses each result to decide what to try next.

The harder part is deciding whether that loop is producing real insight. In research, an experiment can fail because the idea is wrong, because the implementation has a bug, or because you’re measuring the wrong thing. A system needs to distinguish those possibilities rather than just keep trying until it gets a good number.

So I see this developing as a collaboration. Humans provide direction and judgment, while AI makes it much cheaper to explore ideas and test assumptions. Over time, AI may also help us formulate better questions. That’s especially interesting to me, because discovery is not only about finding an answer faster; it’s also about recognizing a question we didn’t know we should ask.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human direction and judgment, but does not identify biological needs as limiting the time humans can devote to research.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes well-defined problem solving from choosing worthwhile problems and describes human–AI collaboration, but does not clearly distinguish automating tedious labor from independently discovering new insights.
